spans.assertion: a Bayesian hierarchical binomial regression model suggests soccer referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players
analyzed dyadic data from 1,433 soccer players in the top male divisions of England, France, Germany and Spain (2012-2013) and 2,906 referees they encountered during their careers
used red-card counts as the outcome variable, controlled for player position and referee country of origin, and estimated the skin-tone effect using a bayesian hierarchical binomial regression model
the model revealed an approximately linear trend, with darker-toned players more likely to receive a red card
soccer referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players
modeled the probability of a player receiving a red card from a given referee in a single game using binomial logistic regression corrected for overdispersion (Gelman & Hill, 2007)
fit different versions of the model to analyze the effect of various combinations of input variables on the main effect of interest, player skin tone
fit preliminary versions of the model using the lme4 R package (version 1.1-6) (Bates, Maechler, Bolker & Walker, 2014)
preliminary fits suggested many input variables (player height, weight, age, games won/lost) don't significantly influence red-card probability, nor significantly change the skin-tone effect estimate
chose a final set of predictors and implemented/fit the definitive models using Stan (version 2.3.0) (Stan Development Team, 2014)
gave unmodeled parameters weakly informative priors and fit each model using four chains with 200 warm-up and 500 effective iterations, no thinning
all models exhibited good convergence (Rhat <=1.05 and n_eff > 100 for the great majority of parameters)
reported the resulting parameters of interest as point estimates (posterior mean) together with 95% credible intervals

spans.note: referees have discretion in judging whether a foul is mild or serious under soccer rules

spans.assertion: modeled the occurrence of a red card as the outcome of a Bernoulli trial, based on referee discretion, independence of a red card from prior cards, and the rule limiting a player to one red card per game
modeled the probability that player i receives a red card from referee j during a game as Bernoulli distributed, using a double subscript to reflect the player-referee pairing structure of the data

spans.note: dataset records the number of games between each player-referee dyad but not how much time the player spent in-game

spans.assertion: assumed every game within a player-referee dyad carries the same weight (since in-game playing time data was unavailable) and generalized the model to a binomial distribution using the dyad's game count
modeled the total red-card count in a player-referee dyad as binomial with number of trials N equal to the number of games and probability of "success" equal to the probability of a red card

spans.note: states the goal of assessing whether player skin tone influences the probability a referee gives a red card

spans.assertion: modeled the red-card probability parameter via an inverse-logit link applied to a baseline probability plus a player skin-color effect, controlling for different predictors across model versions, with an added error term for overdispersion
used a transformed, single-variable combination of the skin-tone rating for the first version of the model
averaged the two raters' skin-tone scores
rounded the averaged skin-tone score to the most central value, applying a conservative rating when the two raters disagreed, to obtain a single skin-tone variable
the resulting averaged/rounded skin-tone variable agreed with 83% of the first rater's ratings and 93% of the second rater's ratings
added the skin-tone rating to the model as a categorical predictor to account for possible non-linearity of the skin-tone effect
added player position and country league as non-nested group-level predictors

spans.note: rationale for including player position (role affects foul rate) and league country (leagues differ in strictness) as predictors

spans.assertion: did not add any interaction term to the regression, because the model suffers from sparse data (red cards are rare events and per-predictor effects are very small)

spans.note: transition into a formal model equation
blank space corresponding to a model equation not captured as text

spans.assertion: excluded all cases with missing data from the analysis
assumed the missingness mechanism was completely at random and performed a complete-case analysis, retaining 115,457 cases (79%)

spans.note: flags that the missing-completely-at-random assumption is strong and might not hold

spans.assertion: most of the missing data comes from the English and French leagues
the first model's skin-tone coefficients showed an almost linear trend, visible in the accompanying graph
in response to the apparent linear trend, changed the model to include skin-tone rating as a numerical predictor at the second level while keeping it categorical at the first level

spans.note: blank space corresponding to a model equation not captured as text

spans.assertion: designed the change so categorical skin-tone estimates could be pulled toward linearity if supported by the data (Gelman & Hill, 2007)
the resulting coefficients didn't change much from the first version, but the 95% credible intervals now excluded 0 for the two extreme skin-tone levels

transformed to odds ratios, level coefficients were 0.89, 0.93, 1.00, 1.05 and 1.12 for levels 1-5 respectively, relative to a mean-odds baseline of 0.0039; in probability terms results differ little since odds are small

the model predicts a mean red-card probability of 0.0039; a light-skin-toned player (level 1) has 11% less chance (0.0034) and a dark-skin-toned player (level 5) has 12% more chance (0.0043) than average
to answer the second research question, selected cases with mean skin-tone rating higher than 3, yielding 15,953 cases
excluded the skin-tone variable from the model predictors since the data were restricted to dark-skin-toned players
included referee country of origin, plus countries' implicit and explicit racial-bias scores (multiplied by 10) as second-level predictors

spans.note: blank space corresponding to a model equation not captured as text

spans.assertion: estimated country effects didn't vary much (sigma = 0.07 [0.00, 0.27])

all 95% credible intervals for country effects included 0; implicit racial bias appeared to have a bigger weight on country effect than explicit bias, but the credible interval was too wide to be convincing evidence
redefined the model for the final approach per peer-review suggestions, excluding the league-country variable because dyad data doesn't come only from a player's current league
changed the skin-tone rating to a 0-1 scale that retained the original five levels
combined the two raters' scores into a single mean value without rounding
included the mean skin-tone rating directly as a numerical predictor, based on the initial approach's suggestion of a linear trend
included referee country of origin in the model
excluded cases with missing data in the variables of interest as before, leaving 116,014 cases (79.4% of the total)
fit a first final-approach model estimating the player skin-tone coefficient as a fixed effect

with the 0-1 skin-tone scale, the baseline represents the lightest level; a lighter-skin-toned player's odds of a red card in a game are 0.0031 (0.0025, 0.0038), and converting to probabilities changes little since the odds are small
the estimated skin-tone coefficient was 0.27 (0.09, 0.45), meaning fifth-level (dark) skin-tone players have an odds ratio of 1.31 (1.09, 1.57) of receiving a red card versus light-skin-toned players
in probability terms, a player at the lighter end of the scale has a 0.31% chance of a red card per game, versus 0.41% for a player at the darker end, holding all else constant

the predicted probability difference between the scale's extremes changed little compared to the initial approach, and both models agree the skin-tone effect is positive with high certainty, i.e. darker-skin-toned players have a higher probability of receiving a red card
expanded the model so the skin-tone coefficient could vary by referee country of origin, with countries' implicit and explicit racial-bias variables as second-level predictors of that coefficient

spans.note: transition into the final model's formal definition/equation

spans.assertion: this expanded model makes more conservative predictions than the previous one: a player with skin-tone rating 0 has mean odds 0.0029 (0.0022, 0.0036) and a player with rating 1 has mean odds 0.0035 (0.0025, 0.0049)
the point estimate of the country coefficient was above 0 for most countries (76%), but only two countries had 95% credible intervals excluding 0
substantial uncertainty was evident in the second-level coefficients; the expected coefficient for a country with no racial bias (IAT=0, Exp=0) was 0.17 (-2.34, 2.51)
the implicit racial-bias coefficient estimate had a different sign than in the initial approach: -0.05 (-0.83, 0.77)
the explicit racial-bias coefficient showed a higher estimate with less uncertainty: 0.06 (-0.06, 0.19)
the variation in estimates between models, together with their high uncertainty, implies the model and data don't provide enough evidence to answer the second research question
conducted predictive (posterior predictive) model checks using the final approach's extended model (with varying skin-tone coefficients) to verify discrepancies from the original data
as expected, the model performs poorly at predicting the true counts above zero, since red cards are rare events and predicted probabilities are very small even in extreme conditions
instead of checking exact red-card count prediction, analyzed whether simulated datasets present features distinct from the original data
simulated datasets had an equivalent number of red-card counts: original data had 1,480 red cards versus a mean of 1,478 (95% range 1,372-1,590) across 2,000 simulated datasets
the model correctly predicted the number of zeros: 114,557 in the original data versus a mean of 114,600 in the simulated datasets
the model predicted the sparsity of red-card counts well: 1,434 one-red-card cases and 23 two-red-card cases in the original data versus simulated means of 1,430 and 23 respectively
a "null" model containing only the baseline produces similarly good results on these same predictive checks, undermining confidence in them

analyzed the mean proportion of red cards per game grouped by skin-tone rating level; the resulting graph shows the model captures the difference between levels, albeit with greater variation at the higher end of the scale

the final-approach skin-tone coefficient implies darker-skin-toned players have 31% higher odds of receiving a red card than lighter-skin-toned players, with a 95% credible interval (1.09, 1.57) that excludes zero
there is great certainty the coefficient's sign is positive, implying soccer referees are more likely to give red cards to players with darker skin tones

spans.note: notes the effect is small, especially compared to the effects of player position or referee country of origin
